y-m-50-01.title: A rule set by two expressions: how many values are there at the boundary?
y-m-50-01.topic: The condition for a correspondence set by expressions on split intervals to be a function (the value at the boundary point)
y-m-50-01.goal: Know that for a correspondence set by different expressions on each interval to be a function, the value must be fixed to one at the boundary point, make several expressions that satisfy that condition, and say that the condition is a single relation.
y-m-50-01.material: Seoa made a correspondence rule on all real numbers. (If x is 2 or less, y is x+3.) (If x is 2 or more, y is a times x plus b, that is, y=ax+b.) Here a and b are constants not decided yet. Seoa says, "I wrote the expression in two parts, so this is a function." How to read: 'x≤2' means 'x is 2 or less' and 'x≥2' means 'x is 2 or more'. When x is exactly 2, both lines apply.
y-m-50-01.thinking.0: Apply the definition of a function (one y for each x) to the boundary point
y-m-50-01.thinking.1: Make several examples that satisfy a condition
y-m-50-01.thinking.2: Say that the information is lacking and does not fix it to one
y-m-50-01.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: the definition of a function (each x in the domain corresponds to exactly one y) and putting an x value into a linear expression y=ax+b to find the y value (middle school level). The domain is all real numbers.
y-m-50-01.s.s1.prompt: For Seoa's rule to be a 'function', what must hold at x=2?
y-m-50-01.s.s1.hint.0: Examine whether both lines apply when x=2, and how many lines apply when x=0 or x=5.
y-m-50-01.s.s1.hint.1: First find the value when x=2 is put into y=x+3, and then create a situation where the value of the second expression differs at the same x.
y-m-50-01.s.s1.o.a: The slopes of the two expressions must be equal
y-m-50-01.s.s1.r.a: Even if the slopes are equal, if the two lines are shifted up and down from each other, there are two y values at x=2. Compare the values at x=2 for y=x+3 and y=x+4.
y-m-50-01.s.s1.o.b: The y values from putting x=2 into the two expressions must be equal
y-m-50-01.s.s1.o.c: a and b must both be integers
y-m-50-01.s.s1.r.c: Whether a and b are integers has nothing to do with being a function. Check whether you can match the value at x=2 even with a non-integer like a=1.5.
y-m-50-01.s.s1.o.d: x=2 must belong to neither of the two expressions
y-m-50-01.s.s1.r.d: Then there is no value corresponding to x=2, so it cannot be called a function defined on all real numbers. Every x in the domain must have exactly one value.
y-m-50-01.s.s1.explain: x=2 belongs to both lines, so the values from putting it into the two expressions must be equal for y to be fixed to one. Where x is not 2, only one line applies, so there is no problem. The slopes do not need to be equal.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.prompt: Make three pairs (a, b), with different a, that make Seoa's rule a function. However, if the second expression is the same line as the first (y=x+3), splitting the expression has no meaning, so leave that case out.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.hint.0: First calculate the value of the first expression at x=2.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one a first, and set b so that putting x=2 into the second expression gives that value.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are within the range.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please keep a between -10 and 10 and b between -20 and 20.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The values of the two expressions are equal at x=2.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The values of the two expressions differ at x=2. Compare the values you get by putting in x=2.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.ok.c3: It is a different line from the first expression.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.fail.c3: This (a, b) makes the same line as y=x+3.
y-m-50-01.s.s2.explain: At x=2 the value of the first expression is 5, so 2a+b=5 must hold. For example, (2, 1), (0, 5), (-1, 7), (3, -1) are all possible. Once you fix a, b follows.
y-m-50-01.s.s3.prompt: Seoa asks, "Then a and b are fixed to exactly one, right?" Look at the pairs made above, write what relation there is between a and b, and say what more is needed to fix them to one.
y-m-50-01.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate 2a+b for the pairs made above and look for what they have in common.
y-m-50-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write what b becomes when a is fixed, and conversely what a becomes when b is fixed.
y-m-50-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: If you put the pairs you made into the relation you wrote, are they all correct?
y-m-50-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that 'once one of a or b is fixed, the other is fixed too'?
y-m-50-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you give a specific example of the extra information needed (the slope, another point it passes through, etc.)?
y-m-50-01.s.s3.model.0: At x=2 the value of the first expression is 2+3=5, so the second expression must also have 2a+b=5. So b=5-2a, and once you pick an a, b is fixed. So one more value, like a or b, must be given for it to be fixed to one.
y-m-50-01.s.s3.model.1: No, it is not fixed to one. There is only the one condition that the value at 2 is 5, so there are many pairs like (2, 1), (0, 5). A condition like the slope or another point it passes through is needed.
y-m-50-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explains the relation in words and examples without writing it in symbols is also fine.

y-m-50-02.title: Can we know the sign of b from a description of the graph alone?
y-m-50-02.topic: Deciding the signs of the coefficients from a description of the graph of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c (sufficiency of information)
y-m-50-02.goal: Judge which combination among several pieces of information describing a graph in words is enough to decide the signs of the coefficients, and build different functions that satisfy all the descriptions to confirm that the descriptions alone do not fix the function to one.
y-m-50-02.material:
Jimin described the graph of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c (a, b, c are real numbers, a≠0) in words. There is no picture. The expression is read 'y equals a times x squared plus b times x plus c'.
(가) The graph opens upward (is convex downward).
(나) The y-coordinate of the point where it meets the y-axis is 3.
(다) The vertex is to the right of the y-axis. (The x-coordinate of the vertex is positive.)
(라) It meets the x-axis at two different points.
y-m-50-02.thinking.1: Reason about the relation between the vertex position and the signs of the coefficients
y-m-50-02.thinking.2: Make several examples that satisfy the conditions
y-m-50-02.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know that the graph of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c is a parabola, that the sign of a decides the opening direction, that the x-coordinate of the vertex is -b/(2a) (or how to change it into the form y=a(x-p)²+q), and the relation between the number of points where it meets the x-axis and the sign of the discriminant b²-4ac.
y-m-50-02.s.s1.prompt: We want to decide the sign of b (positive or negative). Which description among (가) to (라) must we know together to decide it with the least information?
y-m-50-02.s.s1.hint.0: First write the expression for the x-coordinate of the vertex using a and b.
y-m-50-02.s.s1.hint.1: List all the combinations of signs of (a, b) that make that expression positive.
y-m-50-02.s.s1.r.b: The vertex being on the right means -b/(2a) is positive, which only tells us that a and b have opposite signs. Work out what b is when a is positive and when a is negative.
y-m-50-02.s.s1.r.c: (나) and (라) are about the value of c and the discriminant, so they do not tell the sign of a. Test whether y=-x²+2x+3 with a negative a (c=3, discriminant 16, x-coordinate of the vertex 1) satisfies these three descriptions.
y-m-50-02.s.s1.r.d: (가) tells the sign of a and (나) tells the value of c. Without the left-right position of the vertex, change b with the same a and c and see whether the sign of b is fixed.
y-m-50-02.s.s1.explain: If the x-coordinate of the vertex -b/(2a) is positive (다) and a is positive (가), then b is negative. With (다) alone, we only know that a and b have opposite signs. (나) and (라) are not directly related to the sign of b.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.prompt: Make three quadratic functions with different b that satisfy all of (가) to (라). (Enter the values of a, b, and c.)
y-m-50-02.s.s2.hint.0: Decide c from (나), and decide the signs of a and b from (가) and (다).
y-m-50-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put forward a candidate for a and b one at a time, and calculate b²-4ac directly to check (라).
y-m-50-02.s.s2.fail.c1: It does not satisfy (가). Check the sign of a.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not satisfy (나). Check the y value when x=0.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The vertex is on the right.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.fail.c3: It does not satisfy (다). Check the sign of the x-coordinate of the vertex, -b/(2a).
y-m-50-02.s.s2.ok.c4: It meets the x-axis at two points.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.fail.c4: It does not satisfy (라). Check the sign of b²-4ac.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.ok.c5: The value is within the range.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.fail.c5: Please keep a between -10 and 10 and b between -20 and 20.
y-m-50-02.s.s2.explain: e.g., y=x²-5x+3 (discriminant 13), y=x²-4x+3 (discriminant 4), y=2x²-7x+3 (discriminant 25). Several functions satisfy all four descriptions, so the descriptions alone do not fix the function to one. But the signs and values a>0, b<0, c=3 are all the same.
y-m-50-02.s.s3.prompt: Jimin asks, "With four descriptions, we can fix this function to one, right?" Answer based on the functions you made above, and if it cannot be fixed, also write what more is needed.
y-m-50-02.s.s3.hint.0: Look again at whether the different functions you made in the earlier step all satisfy the descriptions.
y-m-50-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare in a table what those functions have different and what they have in common.
y-m-50-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check with numbers that the two functions you gave satisfy all of (가) to (라)?
y-m-50-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the extra information you need really information that fixes a and b to one? (e.g., the coordinates of another point it passes through)
y-m-50-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state the difference that 'the signs are fixed but the values are not'?
y-m-50-02.s.s3.model.0: No, it cannot be fixed. y=x²-5x+3 and y=x²-4x+3 both satisfy the four descriptions but are different functions. We need more information that fixes a and b, such as the coordinates of another point it passes through.
y-m-50-02.s.s3.model.1: It is not fixed to one. The descriptions only tell the signs and values a>0, b<0, c=3 and do not tell the sizes. There must be more conditions, such as the exact coordinates of the vertex.
y-m-50-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: It did not write the examples as expressions, but the judgment and the needed information are specific.

y-m-50-03.title: Moving then flipping versus flipping then moving: is the result the same?
y-m-50-03.topic: The order of translating a graph and reflecting it in the x-axis (the condition for the results to be the same)
y-m-50-03.goal: Confirm with a counterexample that the resulting graph can differ depending on the order of translation and reflection in the x-axis, find on your own the cases where changing the order gives the same graph, and explain why with the position of the vertex.
y-m-50-03.material:
Let's change the graph of y=x² in two orders.
Method A: First reflect it in the x-axis, then translate it by p in the x direction and q in the y direction.
Method B: First translate it by p in the x direction and q in the y direction, then reflect it in the x-axis.
(Positive p means moving to the right and negative p to the left, and positive q means moving up and negative q down. Reflection in the x-axis means flipping it upside down.)
Minho says, "Even if you change the order, the resulting graph is always the same."
y-m-50-03.thinking.0: Choose representative examples to test the claim
y-m-50-03.thinking.1: Find counterexamples and conditions for it to hold
y-m-50-03.thinking.2: Explain the reason with the position of the vertex
y-m-50-03.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know the graph of y=x² (a parabola opening upward with its vertex at the origin), the translation that moves a point (x, y) by p in the x direction and q in the y direction, and the reflection in the x-axis that moves a point (x, y) to (x, -y).
y-m-50-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the test values (p, q) that can show Minho's statement is wrong. (Cases where the resulting graphs of A and B are different from each other)
y-m-50-03.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one test value and write the vertex coordinates of A and B separately.
y-m-50-03.s.s1.hint.1: Use the fact that if the coordinates of the two vertices differ, the graphs differ too.
y-m-50-03.s.s1.r.a: When p is not 0 and q is 0, write where the vertices of A and B end up. Check whether the vertices are the same in the two methods.
y-m-50-03.s.s1.r.c: If nothing is moved, both methods give the graph of y=x² reflected in the x-axis. With this value you cannot see the difference between the two orders.
y-m-50-03.s.s1.r.e: If you only move sideways, changing the order with the x-axis reflection makes no difference. Find the vertices of the two methods separately.
y-m-50-03.s.s1.explain: A has its vertex at (p, q) and opens downward, and B has its vertex at (p, -q) and opens downward. If q is not 0, the y-coordinates of the vertices differ, so they are different graphs. If q is 0, they are the same whatever p is.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.prompt: This time, conversely, make three pairs (p, q), with different p, for which the result is the same even if the order is changed. p and q are integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.hint.0: Recall the cases in the earlier step where, with a few test values, the vertices of A and B became the same.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.hint.1: Test which of p and q makes the difference between the vertices of A and B.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer within the range.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please keep p and q as integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The vertices of A and B become the same.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The vertices of A and B differ. Compare the y-coordinates of the vertices of the two methods.
y-m-50-03.s.s2.explain: The result of A is y=-(x-p)²+q and the result of B is y=-(x-p)²-q. For the two expressions to be the same, we need q=-q, that is, q=0, and p can be any value.
y-m-50-03.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Minho, using the position of the vertex, why p can be any value but q must be 0 for the result to be the same when the order is changed.
y-m-50-03.s.s3.hint.0: Follow and write the position of the vertex step by step in A and in B.
y-m-50-03.s.s3.hint.1: Think about which coordinate of a point the reflection in the x-axis affects.
y-m-50-03.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., In A the vertex ... in B ...
y-m-50-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the vertex coordinates of A and B specifically, like (p, q) and (p, -q)?
y-m-50-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the movement p in the x direction has nothing to do with the x-axis reflection?
y-m-50-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say why the up-down position changes depending on the order for the movement q in the y direction?
y-m-50-03.s.s3.model.0: In B, we first move the vertex to (p, q) and then flip, so the sign of the y-coordinate of the vertex changes and it becomes (p, -q). In A, we move after flipping, so the vertex is (p, q). For q and -q to be equal, q must be 0, and the movement p in the x direction has nothing to do with the x-axis reflection, so it can be any value.
y-m-50-03.s.s3.model.1: Reflection in the x-axis flips things upside down. If you raise it by q and then flip it, it goes down by q, but if you flip it and then raise it, it stays up. So if q is not 0, the height of the vertex differs, and moving sideways has no effect.
y-m-50-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: It explained in words instead of symbols, but it used the height of the vertex as the reason.

y-m-50-04.title: If a composed function is one-to-one, are both functions one-to-one?
y-m-50-04.topic: What we can say about f and g when the composite function g∘f is one-to-one
y-m-50-04.goal: Find the values of the composite function directly from the given table to test Eunsu's claim, and explain how one part of the claim is broken by a counterexample while the other part holds.
y-m-50-04.thinking.0: Split the claim into two parts and judge each separately
y-m-50-04.thinking.2: Explain the reason for the part that holds
y-m-50-04.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know the definition of a function, finding the value of a composite function (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)), and the meaning of a one-to-one function (two different elements of the domain always correspond to different values). One-to-one correspondence and inverse functions are not used.
y-m-50-04.s.s1.prompt: Find the values of g∘f directly for the f and g above, and choose what this example shows about Eunsu's claim.
y-m-50-04.s.s1.hint.0: Find g∘f(1) and g∘f(2) separately and organize them in a table.
y-m-50-04.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether any of the three values g(a), g(b), g(c) of g are equal to each other.
y-m-50-04.s.s1.o.a: If g∘f is one-to-one, then g must also be one-to-one
y-m-50-04.s.s1.r.a: Compare g(a) and g(c). Check whether this g has a case where two different elements have the same value.
y-m-50-04.s.s1.o.b: In this example, g∘f is not a one-to-one function
y-m-50-04.s.s1.r.b: Calculate g(f(1)) and g(f(2)) directly and check whether they are equal. Look at whether you judged before calculating.
y-m-50-04.s.s1.o.c: Even if g∘f is one-to-one, g may not be one-to-one
y-m-50-04.s.s1.explain: g∘f(1)=g(a)=p and g∘f(2)=g(b)=q, so g∘f is one-to-one. But g(a)=g(c)=p, so g is not one-to-one. So the part of the claim saying 'g too' is broken by this one example. One counterexample can break 'always'.
y-m-50-04.s.s2.hint.0: First write as an expression what g(f(1)) and g(f(2)) must be like for g∘f to be one-to-one.
y-m-50-04.s.s2.ok.c1: All three values are elements of Z.
y-m-50-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Compare g∘f(1)=g(f(1))=u and g∘f(2)=g(f(2))=v. In this case g∘f is not one-to-one.
y-m-50-04.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine one example where f is not one-to-one (f(1)=f(2)) and write the two values of g∘f.
y-m-50-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check from the definition of a function what g gives when the same value is put into g.
y-m-50-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If f were not one-to-one, ...
y-m-50-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: When you 'assumed f is not one-to-one', did you mention two specific inputs and the same value?
y-m-50-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does it include the point that putting that value into g gives the same value out?
y-m-50-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about 'why the same method does not work for g'?
y-m-50-04.s.s3.model.0: If f is not one-to-one, so two different inputs have the same value like f(1)=f(2), then putting them into g also gives g(f(1))=g(f(2)), the same. Then g∘f is not one-to-one. So if g∘f is one-to-one, f must be one-to-one.
y-m-50-04.s.s3.model.1: The values of g∘f are decided by putting the values of f into g. If f gives the same value twice, g gives the same answer for that value, so in g∘f different inputs also give the same output. Then it cannot be one-to-one.
y-m-50-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It explained in words without symbols, but it has both the assumption of the same value and the conclusion.

y-m-50-05.title: Two asymptotes and one point: is the graph fixed?
y-m-50-05.topic: Information needed to fix the graph of the rational function y=a+k/(x-p) (asymptotes and a point it passes through)
y-m-50-05.goal: Judge that the asymptotes alone do not fix the rational function to one, that adding a point it passes through fixes it, and that with more conditions they may conflict; revise or keep your judgment, and make up for yourself which of the conflicting conditions to doubt.
y-m-50-05.material: Information about the graph of one rational function arrives one piece at a time. There is no picture. An expression like 'y equals 3 plus k over (x minus 2)' is read that way. An asymptote is a line that the graph gets endlessly close to but never meets.
y-m-50-05.thinking.0: Revise a judgment as information grows
y-m-50-05.thinking.1: Check whether conditions conflict with each other
y-m-50-05.thinking.2: Compare and evaluate which condition to doubt
y-m-50-05.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know that the graph of the rational function y=k/(x-p)+q (k≠0) has the two lines x=p and y=q as asymptotes, and how to put the coordinates of a point into an expression to match the value.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, judge with the information so far, and when new information comes, decide whether to keep or revise your judgment.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.hint.0: Put each piece of information into the expression and count how many unknowns are left.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.hint.1: Put the new information into the expression found earlier and calculate directly whether it fits.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.info: All that is known about the graph of a rational function is that its vertical asymptote is the line x=2 and its horizontal asymptote is the line y=3. This function has the form y=3+k/(x-2) (k is a nonzero constant).
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: Is the function fixed to one by this information alone?
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.after: Whether k is 2, 5, or -3, the asymptotes are the same, x=2 and y=3. The asymptotes only tell the 'frame' where the graph sits, and do not tell k (how much the graph bends, which quadrants it lies in).
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is fixed. Two asymptotes are given, so k is fixed too
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Even if k is 2 or 5, the asymptotes are the same, x=2 and y=3. Check whether you can tell the value of k just by looking at the asymptotes.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is not fixed. Graphs with different values of k all have these asymptotes
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is not fixed. One more asymptote is needed
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: A rational function of this form has exactly two asymptotes. What is lacking is not the number of asymptotes but another kind of information that fixes k.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Newly given information: this graph passes through the point (0, 1).
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, what is the value of k?
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.1.after: Putting in x=0, y=1 gives 1=3+k/(0-2)=3-k/2, so k=4. The graph is fixed as y=3+4/(x-2), that is, y=(3x-2)/(x-2).
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: When putting x=0, y=1 into the expression, check that you put x=0 into x-2 when calculating. One sign may be off.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Putting one point into the expression creates one equation in k. Think about whether that equation has one solution.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.2.info: More information: this graph also passes through the point (4, 6). But if you put x=4 into y=3+4/(x-2) found earlier, you get y=5.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: How will you take in this new information?
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.2.after: If you keep the asymptote y=3 as it is, no graph passes through both points. If you leave the horizontal asymptote open as y=a, then a=3.5, k=5 gives a graph through both points. Which information to trust should be decided by the source of the information and whether it can be checked.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Rewrite k as 6 and forget the earlier point (0, 1)
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If k=6, then y=0 at x=0, which conflicts with the earlier given point (0, 1). Think about whether there is a reason to throw away the earlier information.
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The information about (4, 6) may have been passed on wrongly, so keep k=4 as it is until it is confirmed
y-m-50-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Trust the vertical asymptote x=2 but consider that the horizontal asymptote may not be y=3, and find it again
y-m-50-05.s.s1.reflect: Look at the process of checking directly against the new information, each time information grew, whether 'the earlier judgment is still right'. Also confirm that there were several possible causes when the information conflicted.
y-m-50-05.s.s2.prompt: Let's look for a rational function y=a+k/(x-2) that passes through both the point (0, 1) and the point (4, 6) and has the vertical asymptote x=2. This time, don't fix the horizontal asymptote as y=3 and treat a as unknown too. Enter a possible (a, k).
y-m-50-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put in (0, 1) to write a relation between a and k, and put in (4, 6) to write another relation.
y-m-50-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how many (a, k) satisfy both relations together.
y-m-50-05.s.s2.fail.c1: If k=0, it is not a rational function. Please use a nonzero number.
y-m-50-05.s.s2.fail.c2: y does not become 1 when x=0. Put (0, 1) into the expression to check.
y-m-50-05.s.s2.fail.c3: y does not become 6 when x=4. Put (4, 6) into the expression to check.
y-m-50-05.s.s2.explain: Substituting the two points gives a-k/2=1 and a+k/2=6; adding gives 2a=7, a=3.5, and subtracting gives k=5. y=3.5+5/(x-2), whose horizontal asymptote is y=3.5, passes through both points. With these conditions there is only one solution.

y-m-50-06.title: If we raise the line, will the number of meeting points keep growing?
y-m-50-06.topic: Number of intersections of the graph of the irrational function y=√(x-1)+2 and the line y=x+k (how it changes with k)
y-m-50-06.goal: Test with concrete values the intuition that the number of intersections changes steadily as a line moves in one direction, find several values that satisfy the condition, and explain that the number of intersections depends on the range of k.
y-m-50-06.material:
The graph of the function f(x)=√(x-1)+2 (x≥1) is a curve that starts at the point (1, 2) and rises slowly toward the right. (√ is read 'square root', and √(x-1) is 'the square root of x minus 1'.) Examples of values: f(1)=2, f(2)=3, f(5)=4, f(10)=5.
We move the line y=x+k (slope 1, k is a constant) up and down. Seohyun says, "If k gets bigger, the line goes up, so the number of points where it meets the graph keeps growing."
y-m-50-06.thinking.0: Test an intuition with concrete values
y-m-50-06.thinking.1: Make several examples that satisfy a condition
y-m-50-06.thinking.2: Explain results that depend on the range
y-m-50-06.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know that the graph of the irrational function y=√(x-p)+q starts at the point (p, q) and curves up toward the right, that the inside of the square root must be 0 or more, the number of roots of a quadratic equation and the discriminant, and viewing the intersections of graphs as solutions of simultaneous equations.
y-m-50-06.s.s1.prompt: Examine the number of points where the line y=x+k meets the graph for k=0, 1, 2. Choose what you can learn about Seohyun's words from the results.
y-m-50-06.s.s1.hint.0: Make a table comparing the values of f(x) and x+k at x=1, 2, 5, 10 for k=0, 1, 2.
y-m-50-06.s.s1.hint.1: In the table, find where the comparison switches between the interval where f(x) is greater than the line and the interval where it is smaller.
y-m-50-06.s.s1.explain: If k=0, the line y=x has f(2)=3>2 and f(5)=4<5, so it meets the graph at one point between x=2 and 5 (one point). If k=1, then f(1)=2=1+1 and f(2)=3=2+1, so they meet at x=1 and x=2 (two points). If k=2, the line is always above the graph and they do not meet (0 points). So the statement 'keeps increasing' is broken by a counterexample.
y-m-50-06.s.s2.prompt: Find three different values of k for which there are exactly two intersections. You may write decimals. (e.g., 1.1)
y-m-50-06.s.s2.hint.0: Make a table, increasing k little by little, to see whether the number of intersections changes somewhere between k=1 and k=2.
y-m-50-06.s.s2.hint.1: Make the same table for values of k less than 1 (0, 0.5, 0.9) and compare the numbers of intersections.
y-m-50-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The line passes at or above the starting point (1, 2).
y-m-50-06.s.s2.fail.c1: For this k, the line passes below the starting point (1, 2) and there is only one intersection.
y-m-50-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The line is low enough to meet the graph twice.
y-m-50-06.s.s2.fail.c2: For this k, the line is too high to have two intersections. (There is one or none.)
y-m-50-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The value is within the range.
y-m-50-06.s.s2.explain: Setting √(x-1)=t (t≥0), we get t+2=t²+1+k, that is, t²-t+k-1=0. To have two different intersections, we need two different non-negative roots. The discriminant is 5-4k>0 and the product of the two roots is k-1≥0, so 1≤k<5/4. If k=5/4 they touch at one point, if k<1 there is one point, and if k>5/4 they do not meet.
y-m-50-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Seohyun what you learned about how the number of intersections changes with k. Give numerical examples, and if you could not find the exact boundary, you may write a guess about between which values it lies.
y-m-50-06.s.s3.hint.0: List, one per line, the values of k and the numbers of intersections you confirmed in the previous two steps.
y-m-50-06.s.s3.hint.1: Looking at what you listed, write in a sentence the order in which the number changes.
y-m-50-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check the number of intersections directly for the values of k you gave?
y-m-50-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why 'keeps increasing' is wrong with at least one value of k?
y-m-50-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state with numbers a guess about about where the boundary (the k where the number of intersections changes) is?
y-m-50-06.s.s3.model.0: For k=0 there was 1, for k=1 there were 2, and for k=2 there were none. So the intersections do not keep increasing as k grows; they increase and then decrease. Somewhere between 1 and 2 it seems to drop from two.
y-m-50-06.s.s3.model.1: The number of intersections depends on k. If k is less than 1, there is one point; if k is from 1 up to less than 1.25, two points; if more than that, they do not meet (at 1.25 they touch at one point). When you raise the line, at first it meets the graph once, then twice, and after that not at all.
y-m-50-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that found the boundary exactly. Even if it could not be found, an explanation with numerical examples is accepted.

y-m-50-07.title: If the wall gets longer, will the pen always get bigger?
y-m-50-07.topic: A restriction of the domain in a maximum problem for a quadratic function (whether the vertex is inside or outside the interval)
y-m-50-07.goal: Judge, depending on the domain condition, whether the maximum of a quadratic function occurs at the vertex or at the end of the interval, revise or keep your judgment when the condition changes, and make a table of the maximum for each condition yourself.
y-m-50-07.material: We build a rectangular pen using all of a 20 m fence. One side is attached to a straight wall, and no fence is used on that side. If the length of the side attached to the wall (the side parallel to the wall) is x m and the length of the side perpendicular to it is y m, then x+2y=20, and the area A=xy (㎡, square meters) is A=x(20-x)/2. (x times '20 minus x', divided by 2) x is greater than 0 and less than 20. The length x of the side attached to the wall cannot exceed the length of the wall.
y-m-50-07.thinking.0: Revise a judgment as conditions change
y-m-50-07.thinking.1: Distinguish the position where the maximum occurs (the vertex or the end of the interval)
y-m-50-07.thinking.2: Organize results for each condition in a table
y-m-50-07.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know the vertex of a quadratic function and finding the maximum on a restricted range (judged from the shape of the graph), and setting up an expression by letting side lengths be letters.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.prompt: Each time the information about the wall's length changes, judge the x that makes the largest pen, and when new information comes, decide whether to keep or revise your judgment.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.hint.0: Make a small table of values of x and A and find where it is largest.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the x that gives the largest value in the table is within the allowed range of x.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.0.info: The wall is very long, so there is no limit on x. (0<x<20)
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which x gives the largest area?
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.0.after: A(5)=37.5, A(10)=50, A(15)=37.5. The graph of A=x(20-x)/2 is a parabola opening downward with its top at x=10, so at x=10 the maximum is 50㎡.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: A(5)=5×15/2=37.5. Calculate one more value to compare what happens to the area when x is increased beyond 5.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: A(15)=15×5/2=37.5. Calculate and compare whether it is smaller than at 10.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.1.info: You found out the wall's length is 8 m. (x is 8 or less)
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, which x makes the largest pen?
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.1.after: The allowed range is 0<x≤8, and the top x=10 is outside the range. Within the range, A grows as x grows, so the maximum is at the endpoint x=8, where A=8×12/2=48 (㎡).
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: x=10 is 2 m longer than the wall, so it cannot be attached to the wall. See how A changes within the allowed range of x.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: In the range where x is 8 or less, calculate whether A grows or shrinks going from x=5 to 8.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.2.info: The wall was moved to a longer place, and the wall's length became 12 m. (x is 12 or less)
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which x makes the largest pen?
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.2.after: The allowed range is 0<x≤12, and the top x=10 is inside the range. The maximum is 50㎡ at the top, and at the end of the wall, x=12, it is 48㎡, which is smaller. Using the wall all the way is not always the best.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: A(11)=11×9/2=49.5. Compare it with the value at x=10.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If you use the wall to its end, A(12)=12×8/2=48. Compare it with the value at x=10.
y-m-50-07.s.s1.reflect: Depending on the wall's length, the maximum sometimes occurred at the 'vertex' and sometimes at the 'end of the interval'. Look back at what you newly checked when you changed your judgment.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.prompt: Make a table of the largest area A (㎡) you can build when the wall's length is w m (0<w≤20). Enter three pairs (w, A) with different maximum areas.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a w, write the allowed range of x, and then find where A is largest in that range.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change w to 4, 8, 12, and so on, and compare how the x that gives the maximum differs.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The wall's length is within the range.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Please keep w greater than 0 and at most 20.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.ok.c2: It is the largest area you can build with that wall.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.fail.c2: This is not the largest area you can build with this w. Look again for where A is largest within the allowed range of x.
y-m-50-07.s.s2.explain: If w is 10 or less, the maximum is at the end of the allowed x, x=w; if w is 10 or more, it is at the top x=10. For example, w=4 gives 32, w=8 gives 48, w=10 gives 50, and w=15 gives 50 (㎡). Different w giving the same area happens when w is 10 or more.
y-m-50-07.s.s3.prompt: Judge whether the statement "The longer the wall, the bigger the pen you can build" is always right, and explain it using the numbers in the table you just made as evidence.
y-m-50-07.s.s3.hint.0: Follow from start to end how the value of A changed as w grew in the table you just made.
y-m-50-07.s.s3.hint.1: Find the value of w where A stops getting bigger.
y-m-50-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., When the wall is 8 m, ..., when it is 15 m, ...
y-m-50-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you speak separately about when the wall is short and when it is long?
y-m-50-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the wall's boundary length (10 m) with a number?
y-m-50-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you recalculate A directly in your numerical examples?
y-m-50-07.s.s3.model.0: If the wall is 8 m, the maximum is 48㎡, and if it is 12 m, it is 50㎡, and even at 15 m it is the same 50㎡. Up to 10 m, a longer wall gives a bigger area, but after that, longer is no use, so 'always' is wrong.
y-m-50-07.s.s3.model.1: It is not always right. With a 4 m wall it is 32㎡ and with 8 m it is 48㎡, growing, but from 10 m and up it stays at 50㎡. The top is at x=10, so even if the wall gets longer than that, the area does not grow.
y-m-50-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that gave the position of the vertex as the reason.

y-m-50-08.title: Eunji's working on the number of intersections: which line is wrong?
y-m-50-08.topic: Number of intersections of the graph of y=|x²-2x-3| and the horizontal line y=m (classified by the range of m)
y-m-50-08.goal: Find the wrong line in a working that examined the number of intersections of the graph of a quadratic function with an absolute value and a horizontal line by the range of m, check by putting in values directly, and correct it.
y-m-50-08.material: This is Eunji's working to find the number of points where the graph of the function f(x)=|x²-2x-3| meets the horizontal line y=m (m is a constant). (|a| is read 'the absolute value of a'.) There is no picture.
y-m-50-08.thinking.0: Find the wrong line in the working
y-m-50-08.thinking.1: Check directly by putting in values
y-m-50-08.thinking.2: Organize by splitting into cases by range
y-m-50-08.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know the graph of a quadratic function (vertex, points where it meets the x-axis), the meaning of the absolute value sign (|a| is -a if a is negative), that the graph of y=|f(x)| is the graph of y=f(x) with the part below the x-axis folded upward, and how to solve a quadratic equation.
y-m-50-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Eunji's working. (Line numbers are shown from 1.)
y-m-50-08.s.s1.hint.0: For m=4, look at whether there is a place on the outer branches (x>3, x<-1), not the folded part, where y becomes 4.
y-m-50-08.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate the values of f(x) at x=3 and x=4 and check whether 4 lies between them.
y-m-50-08.s.s1.line.0: x²-2x-3=(x-3)(x+1), so the graph of y=x²-2x-3 meets the x-axis at x=-1 and x=3, and its vertex is (1, -4).
y-m-50-08.s.s1.line.1: Because of the absolute value, the part that was below the x-axis (-1<x<3) is folded up over the x-axis. The top of the folded part is (1, 4).
y-m-50-08.s.s1.line.2: If m=4, they meet only at the top of the folded part, (1, 4), so there is 1 intersection.
y-m-50-08.s.s1.line.3: If 0<m<4, it meets the folded part at two points and each of the two outer branches at one point, so there are 4 intersections.
y-m-50-08.s.s1.line.4: If m>4, it does not touch the folded part and meets each of the two outer branches at one point, so there are 2 intersections.
y-m-50-08.s.s1.line.5: If m=0, it meets at the two points on the x-axis, x=-1 and x=3, so there are 2 intersections.
y-m-50-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. It is right that for m=4 they meet at the folded top (1, 4), but the two outer branches also pass through y=4. For example, the value is 0 at x=3 and 5 at x=4, so it passes y=4 in between (x=1+2√2). The other side is the same, so there are 3 in all. Lines 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 are correct.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.prompt: Make three different values of m for which there are exactly 4 intersections. You may write decimals.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.hint.0: Start by setting an easy value like m=1 or 2 and count how many points it meets on the folded part and on the outer branches.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.hint.1: As you increase m, find the value where the number of intersections changes for the first time.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a horizontal line above the x-axis.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.fail.c1: If m is 0 or less, there cannot be four intersections. (If m is negative there are none, and if 0 they are points on the x-axis.)
y-m-50-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a horizontal line below the folded top.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.fail.c2: If m is 4 or more, the number of points meeting the folded part decreases. Compare with the height of the folded top.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The value is within the range.
y-m-50-08.s.s2.explain: If 0<m<4, there are two points on the folded part and one point on each of the two outer branches, so 4 in all. If m=0 there are 2, if m=4 there are 3, if m>4 there are 2, and if m<0 there are 0.
y-m-50-08.s.s3.prompt: Write how to check by expressions that there are 3 intersections when m=4. (Solve |x²-2x-3|=4 by splitting it into two cases.)
y-m-50-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write the two numbers that the inside value must be for the absolute value to be 4.
y-m-50-08.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many solutions each quadratic equation has (by the discriminant or by factoring).
y-m-50-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you count the number of x found in each of the two cases and add them?
y-m-50-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you confirm that one case has two solutions and the other case has one solution (a double root)?
y-m-50-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that the x you found are not equal to each other?
y-m-50-08.s.s3.model.0: If x²-2x-3=4, then x²-2x-7=0, so x=1±2√2, which is two; if x²-2x-3=-4, then (x-1)²=0, so x=1, which is one. Together that is 3.
y-m-50-08.s.s3.model.1: |x²-2x-3|=4 means x²-2x-3=4 or x²-2x-3=-4. The first has discriminant 32, which is positive, so two different real roots, and the second has one double root. That is 3 in all, and they are different values.
y-m-50-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that counted using the discriminant.

y-m-50-09.title: The parking sign: how much for 35 minutes?
y-m-50-09.topic: Boundary rules and rounding up for a correspondence whose value changes by interval (a staircase-shaped fee)
y-m-50-09.goal: Notice that a rule given in words does not decide the boundaries of the intervals, so several interpretations are possible, make a fee table that fits one interpretation, and rewrite the wording of the rule so that the interpretation is fixed to one.
y-m-50-09.material:
The sign at the parking lot entrance says this.
"First 30 minutes: 1,000원 / After 30 minutes, 500원 more for every 10 minutes"
Doyun parked for 35 minutes. Hyunsu says, "It's 1,500원," and Daeun says, "It's 1,000원." (The fee is in 원 and the time is in minutes. There is no picture.)
y-m-50-09.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is sufficient
y-m-50-09.thinking.1: Calculate values under one interpretation and make a table
y-m-50-09.thinking.2: Design a rule with no ambiguity yourself
y-m-50-09.prereq.0: 'H1' in this task is only a difficulty label in the production assignment and does not mean the curriculum teaches this content in a particular grade. Premise: assume you already know how to read a function that matches different values to different intervals (a staircase-shaped graph) and the meaning of rounding up (rounding a decimal up to the next integer, e.g., roundup(2.3)=3, roundup(3)=3). In this task, time is treated as a natural number in minutes.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.prompt: Can we say how much Doyun's fee is just from the wording of the sign? Choose the most suitable judgment.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write in one sentence each how Hyunsu and Daeun read 'every 10 minutes'.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the two readings split not only at 35 minutes but also at 31 minutes, 40 minutes, and 41 minutes.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.o.a: It cannot be decided. It is not written whether we add after a full 10 minutes or as soon as a 10 minutes begins
y-m-50-09.s.s1.o.b: It is 1,500원. As soon as 30 minutes is passed, the 500원 for the first 10 minutes is added right away
y-m-50-09.s.s1.r.b: This is an interpretation that read 'every 10 minutes' as adding as soon as it begins. Check whether the wording says it must be read that way.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.o.c: It is 1,000원. The 500원 is added only when a full 10 minutes is completed, so the 5 minutes is not counted yet
y-m-50-09.s.s1.r.c: This is an interpretation that read 'every 10 minutes' as adding only when it is completed. Check whether the wording says it must be read that way.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.o.d: It is 2,000원. There are 5 more minutes left, so 500원 is added twice
y-m-50-09.s.s1.r.d: The time over is 5 minutes, which does not even reach one 10-minute unit. Check whether the wording gives a basis for adding 500원 twice.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.explain: 'After 30 minutes, 500원 for every 10 minutes' does not say whether the 5 minutes over is counted as one (rounding up) or not counted (rounding down). If rounding up it is 1,500원, if rounding down it is 1,000원, so it cannot be decided from the wording alone.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.acc.0: If you fixed the interpretation as 'add for every 10 minutes that has begun (round up)' and said so, that is reasonable. But you should also state that this interpretation is not written on the sign.
y-m-50-09.s.s1.acc.1: If you fixed the interpretation as 'add for every full 10 minutes (round down)' and said so, that is reasonable. But you should also state that this interpretation is not written on the sign.
y-m-50-09.s.s2.prompt: Make a fee table using Hyunsu's interpretation ('after 30 minutes, round the time over up in units of 10 minutes and add 500원 for each', e.g., 31 to 40 minutes is 1,500원). Enter four pairs (t, fee) that give different fees. t is a natural number (minutes) from 1 to 120.
y-m-50-09.s.s2.hint.0: First find the time over 30 minutes, (t-30), and then count how many 10-minute units it counts as (rounding up).
y-m-50-09.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate and compare the number of round-ups for exactly 40 minutes and for 41 minutes.
y-m-50-09.s.s2.ok.c1: The time is a natural number within the range.
y-m-50-09.s.s2.fail.c1: Please keep t a natural number (minutes) from 1 to 120.
y-m-50-09.s.s2.ok.c2: It is the fee that fits this interpretation.
y-m-50-09.s.s2.fail.c2: This is not the fee that fits this interpretation (rounding the time over 30 minutes up in 10-minute units). Calculate again starting from the time over 30 minutes.
y-m-50-09.s.s2.explain: For example, 20 and 30 minutes are 1,000원, 31 to 40 minutes are 1,500원, 41 to 50 minutes are 2,000원, and 51 to 60 minutes are 2,500원. 40 minutes belongs to 31 to 40 minutes, so 1,500원, and at the moment it becomes 41 minutes it turns to 2,000원. Several times give the same fee, so I had you choose different fees.
y-m-50-09.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite the sign's wording so that the fee for 35 minutes can only be read one way. Also write clearly which side the boundary times (30 minutes, 40 minutes, etc.) belong to.

y-m-50-09.s.s3.model.0: Up to the first 30 minutes (including 30 minutes) is 1,000원. After 30 minutes, the time over is rounded up in 10-minute units, and 500원 is added for each 10-minute unit. Example: 40 minutes is 1,500원, 41 minutes is 2,000원.
y-m-50-09.s.s3.model.1: Within 30 minutes of entry, 1,000원. From 31 minutes, 500원 is added each time a 10 minutes begins. That is, 31 to 40 minutes is 1,500원, and 41 to 50 minutes is 2,000원.
y-m-50-09.s.s3.modelNote.1: A wording that chose the round-up interpretation. Conversely, writing 'every time a full 10 minutes is completed' with examples is also accepted.
